intro.en: Core plain radiographs and contrast investigations routinely presented in final-year general surgery practical examination spotter stations, detailing imaging features, clinical anatomy, differentials, and viva voce points.

items.summary: Erect chest or upper abdominal radiograph demonstrating crescentic subdiaphragmatic radiolucency diagnostic of gastrointestinal perforation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Crescentic translucent gas shadow seen beneath the right dome of the diaphragm, separated from lung base by thin diaphragmatic line.
Usually more conspicuous on the right side because the liver provides a solid, uniform radiopaque background.
Left-sided subdiaphragmatic gas must be distinguished from the normal gastric fundic air bubble and splenic flexure gas.
Patient must sit or stand erect for at least 10 to 15 minutes before exposure to permit free gas to ascend under the diaphragm.

blocks.title: Common causes and alternative views
bullets: Most common surgical cause in Indian practice is perforated peptic ulcer (duodenal or prepyloric gastric ulcer).
Other causes include typhoid enteric perforation, traumatic bowel injury, amoebic perforation, and anastomotic dehiscence.
If the patient is too ill or haemodynamically unstable to stand, obtain a left lateral decubitus abdominal radiograph.
Left lateral decubitus view shows free peritoneal air rising over the lateral border of the right lobe of the liver.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Postoperative pneumoperitoneum can persist normally for up to 10 days after exploratory laparotomy.
Chilaiditi syndrome is colonic interposition between liver and diaphragm showing colonic haustra without peritonitis.
Absence of free gas does not rule out perforation; sealed peptic perforation or small leak shows no air in 20% to 30%.

viva.q: Why is an erect chest radiograph preferred over an abdominal film for diagnosing pneumoperitoneum?
viva.a: Erect chest film includes both diaphragmatic domes at the centre of the beam, requires less radiation penetration, and visualises as little as 1 to 2 ml of subdiaphragmatic free air.

viva.q: What is Rigler sign on a supine abdominal film?
viva.a: Visibility of both the luminal inner and serosal outer contours of the bowel wall, seen when large-volume pneumoperitoneum introduces air on both sides of the intestinal wall.

viva.q: How do you distinguish subdiaphragmatic free air from the gastric fundal bubble?
viva.a: Free air forms a thin crescent under the right dome; gastric bubble is on the left, has thicker gastric wall above it, and shows an air-fluid level on erect posture.

image.brief: Plain erect chest radiograph displaying a distinct, thin crescent of radiolucent free air immediately beneath the right hemidiaphragmatic dome over the liver shadow.

credit.author: Cambridge University Press; book figure author not verified

items.summary: Erect and supine abdominal radiograph showing centrally located dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels in a step-ladder pattern.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Centrally located, dilated loops of small intestine exceeding 3 cm in transverse diameter on supine projection.
Valvulae conniventes (plicae circulares) appear as thin mucosal lines traversing the entire transverse diameter from wall to wall.
Erect projection shows multiple air-fluid levels arranged in a classic step-ladder pattern from right iliac fossa to left hypochondrium.
Conspicuous absence or marked paucity of gas shadows in the large colon and rectum indicates complete mechanical blockage.

blocks.title: Common causes and radiological signs
bullets: Postoperative peritoneal bands and adhesions are the single most common cause in adult patients.
Incarcerated or strangulated external hernia; always examine the groin, umbilical, and femoral orifices clinically.
String-of-beads sign represents small collections of gas trapped between mucosal valvulae in fluid-filled small bowel.
Differential fluid levels in the two limbs of the same loop (differential height greater than 5 mm) signifies active peristalsis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: More than 2 to 3 fluid levels in the adult small intestine are pathological on an erect abdominal radiograph.
Jejunum is identified by prominent, closely spaced valvulae conniventes; ileum has featureless, smoother mucosal contours.
Strangulation signs include bowel wall thickening, target sign, pneumatosis intestinalis, or portal venous gas.

viva.q: What is the 3-6-9 rule in plain abdominal film interpretation?
viva.a: Upper limit of normal luminal caliber is 3 cm for small bowel, 6 cm for colon, and 9 cm for the caecum; values above these thresholds indicate pathological dilatation.

viva.q: How do you distinguish small bowel loops from large bowel on a plain radiograph?
viva.a: Small bowel is central with plicae circulares crossing the entire lumen; large bowel is peripheral with haustrations that do not span the complete luminal width.

viva.q: What is the string-of-beads or pearls sign?
viva.a: Small pockets of residual gas trapped between mucosal valvulae conniventes in predominantly fluid-distended bowel loops, virtually diagnostic of mechanical small intestinal obstruction.

image.brief: Plain erect abdominal radiograph demonstrating multiple dilated central small intestine loops with complete transverse mucosal folds and step-ladder air-fluid levels.

credit.author: James Heilman, MD

items.summary: Plain abdominal radiograph showing peripheral colonic luminal distension with preserved haustrations and caecal dilatation proximal to an obstruction.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Peripherally situated, distended bowel along the right flank, epigastrium, and left flank framing the peritoneal cavity.
Haustral folds indenting the colonic lumen at irregular intervals without traversing the complete diameter of the bowel.
Caecal diameter exceeding 9 cm indicates impending or critical risk of caecal blowout perforation.
Absence of gas in the rectum and distal descending colon points to an obstructing lesion in the left colon or rectosigmoid.

blocks.title: Clinical causes and ileocaecal valve status
bullets: Colorectal adenocarcinoma (most common cause in adults over 50 years of age, especially rectosigmoid junction).
Diverticular stricture, colonic volvulus (sigmoid or caecal), and benign inflammatory strictures.
Competent ileocaecal valve creates a closed-loop obstruction between valve and tumour, precipitating massive caecal distension.
Incompetent ileocaecal valve allows colonic decompression retrogradely into small bowel, mimicking small intestinal obstruction.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The caecum has the thinnest wall and greatest radius in the colon, making it most vulnerable to rupture by Laplace law.
A caecal diameter greater than 10 to 12 cm on supine film warrants emergency decompression to prevent faecal peritonitis.
Water-soluble contrast enema (Gastrografin) or contrast CT is useful to delineate the site and nature of the colonic block.

viva.q: Why is the caecum at greatest risk of perforation in large bowel obstruction?
viva.a: By Laplace law (wall tension equals pressure multiplied by radius), the caecum has the widest diameter, generating highest wall tension and highest risk of ischaemic blowout.

viva.q: What is the difference in presentation between a competent and incompetent ileocaecal valve?
viva.a: A competent valve produces closed-loop obstruction with rapid caecal dilation and early perforation; an incompetent valve decompresses into ileum, delaying colonic rupture.

viva.q: What are the commonest causes of mechanical large bowel obstruction in adults?
viva.a: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum accounts for approximately 60% of cases, followed by diverticular stricture and volvulus of the sigmoid colon.

image.brief: Plain supine abdominal radiograph showing marked peripheral dilatation of the ascending, transverse, and descending colon with preserved haustra framing the abdomen.

credit.author: Cambridge University Press; book figure author not verified

aka: Bent inner tube sign in volvulus
items.summary: Plain abdominal radiograph showing an inverted U-shaped, massively distended closed loop of sigmoid colon originating from pelvis towards right upper quadrant.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Massive, ahaustral, gas-filled closed loop of sigmoid colon arising from the pelvis and projecting towards the right upper quadrant.
Coffee-bean sign formed by the apposition of the two medial walls of the twisted loop creating a dense central vertical cleft.
Inverted U-loop or omega loop appearance with complete loss of haustral markings due to severe luminal distension.
The apex of the distended loop typically reaches under the right hemidiaphragm or epigastric region (Frimann-Dahl sign).

blocks.title: Predisposing factors and anatomy
bullets: Common in elderly institutionalised individuals, chronic constipation, neuropsychiatric disease, and high-roughage diet.
Anatomical prerequisites include a long, redundant sigmoid colon with a narrow-based pelvic mesosigmoid attachment.
Torsion occurs clockwise around the narrow mesenteric axis, leading to closed-loop obstruction and strangulation.
Contrast enema demonstrates the classic bird-of-prey or ace-of-spades sign terminating at the site of mesenteric torsion.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Sigmoid volvulus is the most frequent type of colonic volvulus encountered in Indian surgical practice.
Initial management in uncomplicated, non-strangulated volvulus is rigid sigmoidoscopic derotation and flatus tube placement.
Definitive elective resection (sigmoid colectomy) is mandatory following successful decompression because recurrence exceeds 50%.

viva.q: Describe the coffee-bean sign on plain abdominal radiograph.
viva.a: A huge, smooth, inverted U-shaped dilated loop of sigmoid colon whose two adjacent medial walls form a dense central radiopaque stripe resembling a coffee bean cleft.

viva.q: What is the bird-of-prey sign seen on contrast enema in sigmoid volvulus?
viva.a: Smooth, concentric, beak-like tapering of the barium column terminating at the twist point in the rectosigmoid junction, resembling a bird beak or ace of spades.

viva.q: What are the indications for immediate emergency laparotomy in sigmoid volvulus?
viva.a: Presence of peritonitis, systemic toxicity, bloody rectal discharge, failed endoscopic decompression, or evidence of gangrene and perforation on sigmoidoscopy.

image.brief: Plain abdominal radiograph demonstrating a huge, inverted U-shaped ahaustral gas-filled loop extending from pelvis to right upper quadrant with central coffee-bean stripe.

credit.author: Mont4nha

items.summary: Plain abdominal radiograph showing an ectopic, dilated comma-shaped caecum with a single fluid level located in the epigastrium or left upper quadrant.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Single, large, oval or comma-shaped distended gas-filled viscus located ectopically in the epigastrium or left upper quadrant.
Presence of a single prominent air-fluid level within the distended caecal bubble on an erect abdominal projection.
Absence of the normal gas and soft tissue shadow in the right iliac fossa (empty right lower quadrant).
Associated dilatation of distal small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels due to ileocaecal mechanical obstruction.

blocks.title: Mechanism and distinction from sigmoid volvulus
bullets: Results from congenital incomplete embryological fixation and excessive mobility of the caecum and ascending colon.
Caecal bascule variant occurs when the mobile caecum folds anteriorly and superiorly over the ascending colon.
Distinguished from sigmoid volvulus: caecal volvulus has one air-fluid level and empty right fossa; sigmoid has two limbs and arises from pelvis.
Emergency surgical management is right hemicolectomy or caecopexy, as endoscopic decompression is rarely successful and unsafe.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Accounts for approximately 15% to 20% of all colonic volvulus presentations.
Plain abdominal radiograph is diagnostic in approximately 50% to 70% of cases; contrast-enhanced CT confirms the whirl sign.
Right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis is the treatment of choice in both gangrenous and viable cases.

viva.q: How do you differentiate caecal volvulus from sigmoid volvulus on a plain radiograph?
viva.a: Caecal volvulus shows a single air-fluid level in the left upper quadrant with an empty right iliac fossa; sigmoid volvulus displays an inverted U-loop from the pelvis.

viva.q: What is the embryological defect predisposing to caecal volvulus?
viva.a: Failure of normal peritoneal fixation of the ascending colon and caecum to the posterior abdominal wall during the third stage of gut rotation.

viva.q: Why is endoscopic decompression not recommended as first-line therapy for caecal volvulus?
viva.a: Endoscopic success rate is low (under 30%), risk of caecal perforation is high, and strangulation cannot be reliably assessed from the lumen.

image.brief: Plain supine abdominal radiograph showing a large comma-shaped distended gas shadow in the left upper quadrant and absence of normal caecal gas in the right iliac fossa.

credit.author: Cambridge University Press; book figure author not verified

items.summary: Plain radiograph of kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB) demonstrating a radio-opaque calcific density projected over the renal outline at L1-L2 level.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Solitary or multiple radio-opaque shadows overlying the renal silhouette within the paraspinal gutters between T12 and L3.
Right kidney shadow lies slightly lower than the left kidney due to the anatomical mass of the liver.
Density moves synchronously with the renal shadow on respiratory excursion during fluoroscopy or comparative phase radiographs.
On a lateral abdominal film, a renal calculus remains projected posterior to the anterior margin of the lumbar vertebral bodies.

blocks.title: Composition and differential diagnosis
bullets: Approximately 90% of renal calculi are radio-opaque: calcium oxalate (most opaque), calcium phosphate, and struvite.
Uric acid, urate, and xanthine calculi are radiolucent and will not be detected on plain KUB radiography.
Cystine calculi are faintly radio-opaque due to their sulphur content, giving a ground-glass appearance.
Differential diagnosis of right upper quadrant calcifications includes gallstones, calcified mesenteric nodes, and costal cartilage.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Gallstones project anterior to the vertebral bodies on a lateral view, whereas renal calculi project over the vertebral bodies.
Non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT KUB) is the gold standard diagnostic investigation for acute flank pain and suspected stones.
Calculi greater than 2 cm or in the lower pole calyx are standard indications for percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).

viva.q: Which renal stones are radio-opaque and which are radiolucent on plain KUB film?
viva.a: Calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, and struvite stones are radio-opaque; pure uric acid, xanthine, and indinavir stones are radiolucent; cystine is faintly opaque.

viva.q: How do you differentiate a renal calculus from a gallstone on plain radiographs?
viva.a: On lateral view, renal stones project posteriorly over the vertebral column; gallstones lie anterior to vertebrae. Gallstones often show facetting or laminated rings.

viva.q: What is the primary investigation of choice for acute renal colic today?
viva.a: Non-contrast computed tomography of kidneys, ureters, and bladder (NCCT KUB), detecting stones of all compositions down to 1 mm size.

image.brief: Plain KUB radiograph demonstrating a well-defined, dense radio-opaque calculus projected over the lower pole calyx of the right kidney silhouette at the L2 vertebral level.

credit.author: University of Washington Virtual Patient; contributor not identified

items.summary: Plain KUB radiograph demonstrating a large, branched radio-opaque calculus forming a cast of the renal pelvis and extending into major and minor calyces.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Large, dense, branched radio-opaque opacity accurately replicating the anatomy of the renal pelvis and multiple calyces.
Complete staghorn calculus fills the renal pelvis and all calyceal groups; partial staghorn involves pelvis and at least two calyces.
Outlines the calyceal system so clearly that it mimics a retrograde pyelogram or contrast nephrogram on a plain radiograph.
Usually unilateral, but bilateral staghorn stones can occur in chronic neurogenic bladder or recurrent proteus infection.

blocks.title: Etiopathology and composition
bullets: Composed predominantly of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) mixed with calcium carbonate-apatite.
Precipitated by chronic urinary tract infection with urease-producing bacteria (Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas).
Bacterial urease hydrolyses urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, elevating urine pH above 7.2 and precipitating triple phosphates.
Usually presents indolently with dull flank pain, recurrent urinary infection, or painless haematuria rather than acute colic.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Left untreated, staghorn calculi inevitably destroy the renal parenchyma, causing xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis or urosepsis.
Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the surgical treatment of choice, occasionally combined with shock-wave lithotripsy.
Complete stone clearance is essential; any residual infected nidus leads to rapid recurrence.

viva.q: What is the chemical composition and etiology of a staghorn calculus?
viva.a: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and carbonate-apatite, formed in alkaline urine generated by urea-splitting organisms such as Proteus mirabilis.

viva.q: Why do staghorn calculi rarely present with acute ureteric colic?
viva.a: Because they are too large to enter the ureteric orifice; they grow silently in the renal pelvis and calyces causing dull ache or recurrent infection.

viva.q: What is the surgical treatment of choice for a staghorn calculus?
viva.a: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), often using multiple puncture tracts to clear all calyceal extensions and eradicate the infected foreign body.

image.brief: Plain KUB radiograph demonstrating a massive, dense branched radio-opaque staghorn calculus outlining the renal pelvis and multiple calyces of the left kidney.

credit.author: Craterib

items.summary: Plain KUB radiograph demonstrating an oval or elongated radio-opaque shadow along the anatomical course of the ureter.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Small, dense, oval or date-seed shaped radio-opaque shadow aligned vertically along the anatomical line of the ureter.
Ureteric anatomical line runs from tips of lumbar transverse processes (L2 to L5), across sacroiliac joint, to ischial spine.
Long axis of the calculus typically aligns along the longitudinal axis of the ureteric lumen.
Commonest sites of impaction correspond to the three physiological ureteric narrowings.

blocks.title: Sites of impaction and differentials
bullets: Pelviureteric junction (PUJ), crossing of the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, and the narrow vesicoureteric junction (VUJ).
Vesicoureteric junction is the narrowest site (approximately 1 to 2 mm caliber) and the most frequent site of stone impaction.
Distinguish from pelvic phleboliths: phleboliths have a central radiolucent lucency, are multiple, and lie lateral to ischial spine.
Other differentials include calcified pelvic lymph nodes, appendicoliths, and arterial wall calcifications.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Stones less than 5 mm in diameter pass spontaneously in over 70% of cases under conservative medical expulsive therapy.
Medical expulsive therapy includes alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin), adequate hydration, and analgesics.
Ureteroscopy (URS) with holmium laser lithotripsy is the standard intervention for symptomatic or unpassed ureteric stones.

viva.q: What are the three anatomical sites of physiological ureteric constriction?
viva.a: Pelviureteric junction, site where the ureter crosses the common or external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, and the vesicoureteric junction inside the bladder wall.

viva.q: How do you differentiate a lower ureteric calculus from a pelvic phlebolith on plain radiograph?
viva.a: Phleboliths are circular with a characteristic central lucency (doughnut sign) and lie low and lateral; ureteric stones are solid, oval, and lie medial to ischial spine.

viva.q: What is the conservative management protocol for a 4 mm lower ureteric calculus?
viva.a: Hydration, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesia, and medical expulsive therapy with an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin 0.4 mg) for up to 4 weeks with periodic monitoring.

image.brief: Plain KUB radiograph showing a 6 mm oval radio-opaque calculus projected over the right sacroiliac joint line, oriented with its long axis along the ureter.

credit.author: University of Washington Virtual Patient; contributor not identified

items.summary: Plain radiograph of the pelvis demonstrating an oval, laminated radio-opaque calculus situated in the true pelvis above the symphysis pubis.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Dense radio-opaque shadow located in the true pelvis in the midline, directly superior to the pubic symphysis.
Often exhibits concentric laminated rings reflecting successive deposition of minerals and organic matrix.
Typically oval or pyriform in shape with smooth, rounded margins; long axis lies transversely across the pelvic basin.
Calculus changes its anatomical position on tilt views or between erect and supine postures as it rolls in the bladder.

blocks.title: Etiology and clinical signs
bullets: Primary vesical calculi occur in children with nutritional deficiencies and low protein, dehydration states.
Secondary vesical calculi occur in adult men secondary to bladder outlet obstruction: benign prostatic hyperplasia or urethral stricture.
Chronic urinary stasis, neurogenic bladder, foreign bodies (indwelling Foley balloon or non-absorbable sutures) act as a nidus.
Classic presentation is painful terminal micturition, terminal haematuria, and sudden interrupted urinary stream relieved by lying down.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: A stone fixed in position in the lateral pelvic wall suggests incarceration within a bladder diverticulum or prostate.
Jackstone calculus is a specific subtype with spiky radiating projections, composed of calcium oxalate monohydrate.
Management includes endoscopic cystolitholapaxy (mechanical or laser) or open suprapubic cystolithotomy for large stones.

viva.q: What causes the classic symptom of sudden interruption of urinary stream in bladder calculus?
viva.a: The mobile stone rolls towards the bladder neck during micturition, ball-valving and abruptly occluding the internal urethral orifice until the patient shifts posture.

viva.q: Why are bladder calculi commonly laminated on plain radiographs?
viva.a: Concentric rings develop due to episodic mineral deposition alternating with inflammatory matrix layers during recurring cycles of infection and stasis.

viva.q: What concurrent procedure must be planned when treating a secondary bladder calculus in an elderly male?
viva.a: Treatment of the underlying bladder outlet obstruction, typically transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) or visual urethrotomy.

image.brief: Plain pelvic radiograph demonstrating a large, rounded, laminated radio-opaque vesical calculus measuring 4 cm, situated in the midline pelvis above the pubic symphysis.

credit.author: Nevit Dilmen (talk)

items.summary: Barium swallow radiograph demonstrating a massively dilated thoracic oesophagus with smooth, symmetrical distal tapering (bird-beak sign).

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Massive dilatation and tortuosity of the proximal and mid-thoracic oesophagus, often described as mega-oesophagus or sigmoid oesophagus.
Smooth, conical, symmetrical tapering of the terminal barium column at the gastro-oesophageal junction (bird-beak or rat-tail sign).
Conspicuous absence of the normal gastric fundic air bubble on plain chest or upper gastrointestinal film.
Fluoroscopy shows absence of primary progressive peristalsis with disorganized tertiary contractions and delayed barium transit.

blocks.title: Pathophysiology and differentiation
bullets: Caused by degeneration of non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric Auerbach plexus.
Results in incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) and aperistalsis of the oesophageal body.
Distinguish from pseudoachalasia (carcinoma of the gastro-oesophageal junction): malignancy shows mucosal destruction and asymmetry.
High-resolution manometry (HRM) is the modern diagnostic gold standard, categorising achalasia into Chicago types I, II, and III.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Chest radiograph may show widened mediastinum with a mediastinal air-fluid level and absent gastric air bubble.
Definitive surgical treatment is laparoscopic Heller cardiomyotomy combined with a partial anterior (Dor) fundoplication.
Alternative interventions include per-oral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) or pneumatic balloon dilatation.

viva.q: Describe the characteristic radiological findings of achalasia cardia on barium swallow.
viva.a: Dilated oesophagus with loss of primary peristalsis and smooth, symmetrical, cone-shaped tapering at the gastro-oesophageal junction resembling a bird beak or pencil tip.

viva.q: What is the underlying neuro-anatomical defect in primary achalasia cardia?
viva.a: Selective loss or degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells in Auerbach myenteric plexus producing nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide.

viva.q: Why is a partial fundoplication performed after Heller cardiomyotomy?
viva.a: To prevent severe gastro-oesophageal reflux disease created by dividing the lower sphincter, while avoiding total fundoplication which causes severe dysphagia.

image.brief: Barium swallow radiograph demonstrating a markedly dilated, column-like thoracic oesophagus tapering symmetrically into a smooth bird-beak point at the gastro-oesophageal junction.

credit.author: University of Washington Virtual Patient; contributor not identified

items.summary: Barium swallow radiograph showing irregular, asymmetric luminal narrowing with shouldered overhanging margins and destroyed mucosal folds.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Irregular, eccentric, persistent luminal narrowing and constriction involving a discrete segment of the oesophagus.
Classic shouldering sign: abrupt shelf-like transition between normal proximal oesophagus and the constricted malignant segment.
Marked destruction and ulceration of the normal mucosal relief pattern within the narrowed segment (rat-tail appearance).
Proximal oesophagus shows only mild to moderate compensatory dilatation, unlike the massive mega-oesophagus of achalasia.

blocks.title: Pathological types and anatomical sites
bullets: Squamous cell carcinoma is traditionally most common in upper and middle thirds, linked with tobacco and alcohol use.
Adenocarcinoma is increasingly prevalent in the lower third and gastro-oesophageal junction, arising on Barrett columnar metaplasia.
Hold-up of barium with pooling, aspiration into tracheobronchial tree, or fistulous communication may be demonstrated.
Upper gastrointestinal flexible endoscopy with biopsy is mandatory to obtain histological confirmation and staging.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Mild proximal dilatation occurs because carcinoma grows rapidly, causing progressive dysphagia before massive dilation can develop.
Preoperative clinical staging requires contrast-enhanced CT of thorax and abdomen plus endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).
Tracheo-oesophageal fistula manifests as contrast spill into the right or left main bronchus during swallow.

viva.q: What is the shouldering sign on a barium swallow radiograph?
viva.a: Abrupt, shelf-like, right-angled margin where the normal pliable oesophageal wall transitions into the rigid, infiltrative malignant stricture.

viva.q: Why is proximal dilatation mild in oesophageal carcinoma compared with achalasia cardia?
viva.a: Because malignancy causes rapid luminal obstruction over weeks or months, whereas achalasia is a chronic, benign process evolving over many years.

viva.q: What are the common histological types and their typical anatomical distributions in the oesophagus?
viva.a: Squamous cell carcinoma predominates in the upper and middle thirds; adenocarcinoma is most common in the lower third near the gastro-oesophageal junction.

image.brief: Barium swallow radiograph demonstrating an irregular, eccentric stricture in the mid-thoracic oesophagus with sharp shelf-like shouldering and mucosal ulceration.

credit.author: Radiology Assistant; original radiologist/photographer not identified in retrieved result

items.summary: Barium meal radiograph showing an intraluminal filling defect, malignant ulcer crater (Carman meniscus sign), or rigid tubular stomach (linitis plastica).

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Irregular, polypoid, space-occupying intraluminal filling defect protruding into the contrast pool in the antrum or body.
Malignant ulcer crater: large, shallow ulcer lying entirely within the projected contour of the gastric wall, surrounded by nodular halo.
Carman meniscus sign: lenticular lens-shaped barium collection trapped between indurated, elevated rolled edges of a malignant ulcer.
Linitis plastica: tubular, rigid, contracted stomach with complete loss of distensibility and absent peristaltic waves on fluoroscopy.

blocks.title: Differentiation from benign gastric ulcer
bullets: Benign ulcer crater projects outside the expected luminal profile of the stomach wall; malignant ulcer lies inside the profile.
Benign ulcer displays smooth, radiating mucosal folds extending directly to the crater margin (Hampton line).
Malignant ulcer shows truncated, nodular, clubbed mucosal folds terminating abruptly at a distance from the ulcer crater.
Gastric antral carcinoma frequently presents with gastric outlet obstruction, showing massive gastric retention and delayed emptying.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Double-contrast barium meal provides superior mucosal coating, but flexible upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and biopsy is gold standard.
Leather-bottle stomach (linitis plastica) is caused by diffuse infiltrative scirrhous carcinoma (Borrnann type IV).
Contrast CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis is essential for TNM anatomical staging and detection of ascites or hepatic secondaries.

viva.q: What is Carman meniscus sign on a barium meal study?
viva.a: A lens-shaped barium collection convex towards the gastric lumen, produced when compression traps contrast inside a large malignant ulcer surrounded by rolled, elevated borders.

viva.q: How do you radiologically differentiate a benign gastric ulcer from a malignant gastric ulcer?
viva.a: Benign ulcer projects beyond the gastric lumen with smooth radiating folds (Hampton line); malignant ulcer sits within the luminal contour with irregular, clubbed, amputated folds.

viva.q: What are the radiological hallmarks of linitis plastica?
viva.a: A small, rigid, non-distensible, tubular stomach with absent peristalsis, thick unyielding walls, and rapid emptying into the small intestine.

image.brief: Double-contrast barium meal radiograph demonstrating a large intraluminal filling defect in the gastric antrum with irregular mucosal destruction and persistent ulcer crater.

items.summary: Barium meal radiograph showing a persistent contrast collection (ulcer niche) in the duodenal cap with radiating mucosal folds and clover-leaf deformity.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Persistent, dense barium fleck or collection (ulcer niche or crater) visualised within the duodenal bulb (cap).
Radiating mucosal folds converging symmetrically like spokes of a wheel towards the central ulcer crater.
Clover-leaf (trefoil) deformity of the duodenal cap caused by cicatricial scarring, fibrosis, and pseudodiverticular sacculations.
Associated localized spasm of the duodenal bulb (irritable cap) with rapid transit or persistent deformity on serial compression films.

blocks.title: Clinical complications visible on contrast films
bullets: Over 95% of duodenal ulcers arise in the first part of the duodenum within 3 cm of the pyloric ring, mostly anterior or posterior.
Chronic scarring leads to pyloric stenosis or gastric outlet obstruction with marked gastric dilatation and succussion splash.
Posterior wall duodenal ulcers penetrate into the pancreas, eroding the gastroduodenal artery to cause massive haematemesis.
Anterior wall duodenal ulcers perforate freely into the peritoneal cavity, causing pneumoperitoneum and generalised peritonitis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Duodenal ulcers are almost invariably benign; malignant duodenal ulcers are exceedingly rare.
Helicobacter pylori eradication and proton-pump inhibitors have drastically reduced the need for elective ulcer surgery.
Barium study is contraindicated in suspected acute perforation due to chemical peritonitis risk; use water-soluble contrast if needed.

viva.q: What causes the clover-leaf (trefoil) deformity of the duodenal bulb?
viva.a: Fibrotic cicatricial contraction and scarring from chronic recurring duodenal ulceration, forming pseudodiverticular outpouchings between puckered fibrous bands.

viva.q: What is the difference in complication between anterior and posterior duodenal ulcers?
viva.a: Anterior duodenal ulcers perforate freely into the peritoneal cavity causing peritonitis; posterior ulcers penetrate into the pancreas and erode the gastroduodenal artery causing bleeding.

viva.q: Why is barium sulphate contraindicated in suspected gastrointestinal perforation?
viva.a: Extravasated barium sulphate in the peritoneal cavity causes severe, granulomatous foreign-body peritonitis with extensive adhesions and high mortality.

image.brief: Barium meal radiograph demonstrating a trifoliate, clover-leaf deformed duodenal bulb with a central dense barium ulcer niche and mucosal fold convergence.

credit.author: University of Washington Virtual Patient; contributor not identified

title.en: Carcinoma colon on barium enema (Apple-core sign)

aka: Annular colonic carcinoma on contrast enema
items.summary: Double-contrast barium enema showing an annular, circumferential luminal constriction with overhanging shelf-like edges (apple-core appearance).

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Short, sharply demarcated segment of severe circumferential luminal narrowing typically 3 to 5 cm in longitudinal length.
Overhanging, shelf-like margins (shoulders) at both proximal and distal transitions into normal bowel (apple-core deformity).
Complete loss of normal mucosal relief pattern with jagged, irregular, ulcerated channel through the constricted segment.
Proximal colon demonstrates compensatory distension with delayed barium filling or complete retrograde obstruction.

blocks.title: Anatomical distribution and pathology
bullets: Annular constricting lesions are classic for the left colon (descending colon, sigmoid, and rectosigmoid junction).
Left-sided lesions cause early alteration in bowel habits, progressive constipation, colicky pain, and obstruction.
Right-sided colonic tumours (caecum, ascending colon) tend to be large, polypoid, fungating masses presenting with anaemia.
Colonoscopy with endoscopic biopsy is the definitive diagnostic modality for histological confirmation.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Double-contrast enema uses barium suspension for mucosal coating and insufflated air for distension.
Barium enema must never be performed during acute diverticulitis or acute colonic obstruction due to perforation risk.
CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy) has largely replaced conventional barium enema in modern diagnostic practice.

viva.q: What produces the apple-core appearance in colonic carcinoma?
viva.a: Circumferential annular tumour growth constricting the colonic lumen, with sharp overhanging proximal and distal margins resembling an apple core eaten down to its center.

viva.q: How does the clinical presentation of right-sided colonic cancer differ from left-sided cancer?
viva.a: Right-sided cancer presents with iron deficiency anaemia, occult bleeding, and palpable mass; left-sided cancer causes altered bowel habits, pencil stools, and obstruction.

viva.q: What are the contraindications to performing a barium enema?
viva.a: Suspected colonic perforation, toxic megacolon, acute fulminant colitis, acute diverticulitis, and recent deep endoscopic biopsy.

image.brief: Double-contrast barium enema radiograph demonstrating a short, concentric annular stricture in the sigmoid colon with sharp overhanging margins resembling an apple core.

credit.author: Histopathology.guru; photographer not identified

items.summary: Contrast enema radiograph demonstrating a narrow aganglionic distal rectal segment with a funnel-shaped transition zone leading to proximal megacolon.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Narrowed, spastic, non-distensible distal rectum and rectosigmoid segment representing the aganglionic segment.
Funnel-shaped or cone-shaped transitional zone flaring out from the narrow aganglionic zone into dilated proximal bowel.
Massive dilatation and hypertrophy of the normally innervated proximal colon (megacolon) packed with retained faeces.
Reversal of the normal rectosigmoid ratio (normal rectum is wider than the sigmoid colon; in Hirschsprung, rectum is narrower).

blocks.title: Pathophysiology and diagnostic rules
bullets: Caused by congenital failure of cranio-caudal migration of neural crest-derived neuroblasts into the distal bowel.
Absence of ganglion cells in both myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses with hypertrophied nerve trunks.
Do not perform vigorous bowel washouts prior to contrast enema, as washing distorts the diagnostic transitional zone.
Full-thickness rectal biopsy or suction rectal biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells and elevated acetylcholinesterase is definitive.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Classic presentation in a neonate is delayed passage of meconium past 48 hours, abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting.
Digital rectal examination reveals a snug, tight anal canal followed by an explosive gush of liquid stool and flatus upon withdrawal.
Definitive surgical procedures include Duhamel, Soave endorectal pull-through, or Swenson transanal endorectal pull-through.

viva.q: What is the rectosigmoid ratio and how does it change in Hirschsprung disease?
viva.a: Normally, the maximal rectal diameter is greater than the sigmoid diameter (ratio > 1); in Hirschsprung disease, the rectosigmoid ratio is reversed (less than 1).

viva.q: Why should bowel enemas or washouts be avoided immediately before a diagnostic contrast enema?
viva.a: Pre-procedure rectal washouts artificially dilate the aganglionic distal rectum, effacing the characteristic cone-shaped transition zone.

viva.q: What is the definitive investigation for establishing the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease?
viva.a: Rectal suction or full-thickness biopsy obtained at least 2 cm above the dentate line, showing absence of ganglion cells and acetylcholinesterase positivity.

image.brief: Contrast enema radiograph demonstrating a narrow, spastic distal rectosigmoid transitioning via a funnel-shaped cone into a hugely distended, faeces-filled descending colon.

credit.author: Cambridge University Press; book figure author not verified

items.summary: Intravenous urogram demonstrating delayed excretion, pelvicalyceal blunting (clubbing of calyces), and marked dilatation of the renal pelvis.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Delayed nephrogram and delayed appearance of contrast in the collecting system on sequential timed post-injection films.
Progressive loss of normal cup-shaped calyceal concavity (cupping) followed by flattening and globular clubbing of minor calyces.
Marked enlargement and sacculation of the renal pelvis with abrupt cut-off at the pelviureteric junction (PUJ).
Normal, non-dilated caliber of the ureter below the pelviureteric junction confirms primary pelviureteric junction obstruction.

blocks.title: Stages of calyceal changes and etiology
bullets: Normal: sharp, pointed calyceal fornices with cup-shaped hollows embracing the renal papillae.
Grade 1: flattening of calyceal cups; Grade 2: blunting and clubbing of calyces; Grade 3: ballooning into cystic sacs with parenchymal atrophy.
Congenital PUJ obstruction is most common, caused by aperistaltic intrinsic muscle segment or lower polar crossing aberrant vessel.
Secondary causes include impacted ureteric calculus, transitional cell carcinoma, retroperitoneal fibrosis, and stricture.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Check patient history for iodine allergy, asthma, and baseline serum creatinine before administering iodinated contrast media.
Diuretic renography (technetium-99m MAG3 or DTPA scan) provides quantitative functional split renal function and drainage curves.
Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty (open or laparoscopic/robotic) is the surgical gold standard for PUJ obstruction.

viva.q: Describe the chronological progression of calyceal changes in hydronephrosis on IVU.
viva.a: Progression advances from normal sharp cupping to flattening of fornices, followed by blunting, globular clubbing, and finally total ballooning with cortical thinning.

viva.q: What causes primary congenital pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction?
viva.a: An intrinsic aperistaltic, fibrotic segment of the upper ureter, or extrinsic compression by an aberrant lower-pole renal artery crossing the PUJ.

viva.q: What is the surgical gold standard procedure for repairing pelviureteric junction obstruction?
viva.a: Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty, resecting the redundant pelvis and aperistaltic junction with spatulated, tension-free pelviureteric anastomosis.

image.brief: Intravenous urogram 30-minute radiograph demonstrating a grossly dilated, ballooned left renal pelvis and clubbed calyces with abrupt cut-off at the PUJ and no ureteric filling.

credit.author: Cambridge University Press; book figure author not verified

items.summary: Postoperative radiograph following water-soluble contrast injection through a rubber T-tube outlining the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Radiopaque rubber or silicone T-tube visible with horizontal limbs inside the common bile duct and vertical stem exiting skin.
Uniform opacification of the common hepatic duct, common bile duct, and left and right intrahepatic hepatic duct branches.
Free, unobstructed flow of contrast into the second part of the duodenum with a mucosal brush-border mucosal pattern.
Absence of radiolucent filling defects, smooth normal ductal caliber (under 8 to 10 mm), and no contrast extravasation.

blocks.title: Procedure technique and timing
bullets: Routinely performed on the 7th to 10th postoperative day following open choledochotomy and common bile duct exploration.
Performed under fluoroscopic guidance using 30% to 50% water-soluble iodinated contrast (diatrizoate or iohexol).
Crucial precautions: exclude air bubbles from the syringe and tube, as air bubbles mimic retained radiolucent gallstones.
Inject slowly under low pressure without forcing, to prevent cholangiovenous reflux and postoperative acute cholangitis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: If the cholangiogram is completely normal, the T-tube is clamped for 24 hours to test biliary tolerance; if no pain/fever, it is removed.
T-tube is removed by gentle, continuous traction around postoperative day 10 to 14 after a mature fibrous fistulous tract forms.
Retained stone appears as a mobile, rounded radiolucent filling defect with an upper concave contrast meniscus sign.

viva.q: What are the criteria for a normal postoperative T-tube cholangiogram?
viva.a: Uniform filling of intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts without filling defects or strictures, normal duct caliber, and rapid, free spill of contrast into the duodenum.

viva.q: Why must air bubbles be scrupulously avoided during T-tube contrast injection?
viva.a: Because injected air bubbles appear as round radiolucent filling defects in the bile duct that closely mimic retained choledocholithiasis.

viva.q: When and how is a T-tube safely removed following a normal postoperative cholangiogram?
viva.a: At 10 to 14 days post-surgery, ensuring a mature peritoneal tract has formed around the tube to prevent intra-abdominal bile peritonitis upon removal.

image.brief: Postoperative T-tube cholangiogram radiograph showing normal intrahepatic branching, non-dilated common bile duct, and free contrast spill into the duodenal C-loop without filling defects.

credit.author: Hellerhoff

aka: Retained common bile duct stone on cholangiogram
items.summary: Operative cholangiogram demonstrating a rounded radiolucent filling defect with a classic meniscus sign and proximal duct dilatation in the common bile duct.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Dilated extrahepatic common bile duct (diameter exceeding 10 mm) proximal to an obstructed intraluminal segment.
Well-defined, rounded or faceted radiolucent filling defect located in the dependent distal part of the common bile duct.
Classic meniscus sign: the upper convex border of the calculus is outlined by an overarching crescent of radiopaque contrast.
Complete cut-off or severe attenuation of contrast passage into the duodenum with failure of sphincter of Oddi transit.

blocks.title: Indications for intraoperative cholangiography
bullets: Performed during open or laparoscopic cholecystectomy via a cannula inserted into the cystic duct.
Indicated for suspected choledocholithiasis, dilated common bile duct, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin.
Delineates aberrant biliary anatomy (e.g. accessory right hepatic duct entering cystic duct) to prevent bile duct injury.
Provides immediate confirmation of bile duct clearance after choledocholithotomy or laparoscopic CBD exploration.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Distinguish from spasm of the sphincter of Oddi: glucagon 1 mg IV relieves physiological sphincter spasm, restoring duodenal flow.
Distinguish from ampullary carcinoma: malignant tumours cause an irregular, shelf-like, shouldered cut-off rather than smooth meniscus.
Modern alternative for suspected choledocholithiasis is preoperative or postoperative endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

viva.q: What is the meniscus sign on a cholangiogram?
viva.a: A crescentic, cup-shaped contrast shadow capping the upper convex surface of a radiolucent gallstone impacted in the lumen of the common bile duct.

viva.q: How do you differentiate sphincter of Oddi spasm from an impacted distal CBD calculus during surgery?
viva.a: Intravenous administration of glucagon (1 mg) relaxes sphincter spasm and allows prompt contrast transit into the duodenum, but has no effect on a stone.

viva.q: What are the options if an unexpected CBD stone is identified on intraoperative cholangiogram during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
viva.a: Laparoscopic transcystic or choledochotomy stone extraction, conversion to open exploration, or placement of a drain followed by postoperative endoscopic ERCP.

image.brief: Operative cholangiogram radiograph demonstrating a dilated common bile duct with an inverted meniscus filling defect capping a 1 cm stone in the distal duct and absent duodenal flow.

credit.author: Rebekah M. Padilla, Paul C. Hulsberg, Erik Soule, Taylor S. Harmo , Erik Eadie, Preston Ho

items.summary: Chest radiograph demonstrating hyperlucent hemithorax devoid of lung markings, complete pulmonary collapse, depressed diaphragm, and contralateral mediastinal shift.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Markedly increased radiolucency (hyperlucency) of the affected hemithorax completely devoid of pulmonary bronchovascular markings.
Complete collapse of the ipsilateral lung into a small, shrivelled, dense soft tissue stump at the pulmonary hilum.
Marked shift of the trachea, cardiac silhouette, and mediastinum towards the contralateral (healthy) hemithorax.
Severe flattening or downward inversion (depression) of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragmatic dome with widened intercostal spaces.

blocks.title: Clinical emergency priority and causes
bullets: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate emergency needle decompression; NEVER wait for an X-ray in an unstable patient.
Caused by a one-way flap-valve mechanism allowing air entry during inspiration but preventing exit during expiration.
Progressive intrapleural pressure elevation collapses vena cava, severely reducing venous return, causing obstructive shock and cardiac arrest.
Common surgical causes include penetrating chest trauma, fractured ribs tearing visceral pleura, ruptured bulla, and barotrauma.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Classic clinical signs: severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, and hyper-resonance on percussion.
Immediate emergency intervention is needle decompression using a wide-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line or 5th space anterior axillary line.
Definitive management is immediate tube thoracostomy (intercostal drain) connected to an underwater seal drainage bottle.

viva.q: Why is tension pneumothorax described as a clinical diagnosis rather than a radiological diagnosis?
viva.a: Because delaying treatment to obtain a chest radiograph in a haemodynamically unstable patient can cause rapid cardiovascular collapse and fatal cardiac arrest.

viva.q: Explain the mechanism of hypotension and obstructive shock in tension pneumothorax.
viva.a: Progressive positive intrapleural pressure shifts the mediastinum, kinks the superior and inferior vena cavae, drastically falls cardiac venous return, causing shock.

viva.q: What is the immediate life-saving procedure for suspected tension pneumothorax?
viva.a: Immediate needle thoracocentesis with a large-bore cannula (14G) inserted in the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line, followed by formal tube thoracostomy.

image.brief: Erect chest radiograph demonstrating marked hyperlucency of the right hemithorax with absent lung markings, complete right lung collapse, depressed right diaphragm, and leftward tracheal shift.

credit.author: SlideShare uploader not verified

items.summary: Erect chest radiograph demonstrating dense homogeneous opacity in the hemithorax with a concave upper border (Ellis meniscus) and blunting of costophrenic angles.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Dense, homogeneous radiopacity occupying the dependent lower hemithorax, obliterating the costophrenic and cardiophrenic angles.
Classic Ellis S-shaped curved meniscus line: higher laterally in the axilla and curving downwards and medially towards the spine.
Large or massive effusion causes tracheal, cardiac, and mediastinal shift towards the contralateral (healthy) hemithorax.
Loculated effusion or empyema produces an encapsulated, D-shaped or lenticular peripheral opacity with obtuse angles to the chest wall.

blocks.title: Surgical causes and differential
bullets: Post-pneumonic empyema thoracis, tuberculous pleural effusion, haemothorax secondary to chest trauma, and malignant effusion.
Distinguish from pulmonary consolidation: consolidation shows air bronchograms and preserves costophrenic angles without mediastinal shift.
Distinguish from complete lung collapse: collapse pulls trachea and mediastinum towards the affected side; effusion pushes it away.
Thoracocentesis (diagnostic pleural tap) differentiates transudate from exudate using Light criteria and assesses frank pus in empyema.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: At least 150 to 200 ml of pleural fluid must accumulate before costophrenic angle blunting becomes visible on an erect PA film.
Ultrasonography of the thorax is highly sensitive (detects 5 to 10 ml), identifies fibrin septations, and guides safe needle insertion.
Empyema thoracis stages: exudative (early), fibrinopurulent (loculated), and organising (fibrothorax requiring surgical decortication).

viva.q: How do you distinguish massive pleural effusion from total lung collapse on a chest radiograph?
viva.a: Massive effusion pushes the trachea and mediastinal structures to the opposite side; total lung collapse pulls the trachea and mediastinum towards the ipsilateral side.

viva.q: What is the Ellis S-shaped curved meniscus line and why does it form?
viva.a: A concave upward fluid line higher in the axilla, produced by negative intrathoracic pressure and capillary action drawing fluid up the parietal pleura.

viva.q: What are the three stages of empyema thoracis, and which stage requires open or VATS decortication?
viva.a: Exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organising stages; the organising stage with a thick restrictive fibrous peel requires decortication to re-expand the lung.

image.brief: Erect posteroanterior chest radiograph demonstrating dense homogeneous opacity in the lower two-thirds of the right hemithorax with a concave meniscus and blunted costophrenic angle.

items.summary: Chest radiograph demonstrating segmental fractures of three or more consecutive ribs at two sites with extensive radiolucent subcutaneous gas streaks.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Segmental fractures of at least three consecutive ribs in two or more separate locations along each rib arch.
Disruption of normal thoracic contour with inward displacement or paradoxical segment collapse.
Surgical emphysema appears as extensive, striate, radiolucent gas streaks dissecting through the subcutaneous tissues and pectoralis muscle.
Associated underlying pulmonary contusion manifests as patchy, non-segmental, fluffy alveolar opacities.
Frequent co-existing pneumothorax, haemothorax, or clavicular and scapular fractures from severe blunt trauma.

blocks.title: Pathophysiology and paradoxical respiration
bullets: Flail segment moves paradoxically: indrawing during inspiration (negative pleural pressure) and outward bulging during expiration.
Severe hypoxaemia is primarily caused by the underlying pulmonary contusion (alveolar haemorrhage and oedema) rather than paradoxical motion alone.
Pendelluft phenomenon refers to shunting of stale, deoxygenated gas between lungs during paradoxical respiratory movements.
Surgical emphysema results from fractured rib ends puncturing both visceral and parietal pleura, tracking air into chest wall tissues.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Management focuses on aggressive multi-modal analgesia (thoracic epidural or paravertebral block), chest physiotherapy, and oxygenation.
Avoid fluid overload, as excessive crystalloid resuscitation worsens pulmonary contusion (leaky capillaries).
Surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) with titanium plates and screws is indicated for severe deformity, flail chest, or failed weaning.

viva.q: Define flail chest and describe its classic mechanical breathing defect.
viva.a: Fracture of three or more consecutive ribs in two or more places producing a floating thoracic segment that moves paradoxically inward on inspiration and outward on expiration.

viva.q: What is the primary cause of life-threatening hypoxaemia in a patient with flail chest?
viva.a: The underlying pulmonary parenchymal contusion causing alveolar flooding, haemorrhage, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and reduced pulmonary compliance.

viva.q: How does surgical subcutaneous emphysema appear on a chest radiograph?
viva.a: As linear and reticular radiolucent gas streaks dissecting between fascial planes, subcutaneous fat, and muscle fibres of the thoracic wall and neck.

image.brief: Plain chest radiograph showing multiple double fractures of the 4th, 5th, and 6th right ribs with thoracic wall deformity, underlying pulmonary contusion, and chest wall subcutaneous gas.

credit.author: SlideShare uploader not verified

title.en: Colles fracture of the distal radius

aka: Dinner fork deformity fracture on film
items.summary: Plain wrist radiograph showing an extra-articular transverse fracture of the distal radial metaphysis within 2.5 cm of articular surface with dorsal displacement and tilt.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Transverse fracture line across the distal radial metaphysis situated within 2.5 cm (1 inch) of the radiocarpal articular surface.
Dorsal displacement: the distal fragment is shifted bodily backwards relative to the radial shaft on lateral projection.
Dorsal tilt (dorsal angulation): the articular surface tilts backward instead of its normal 10 to 12 degree palmar tilt.
Radial shift and radial tilt: the distal fragment tilts towards the radial styloid with disruption of radial height.
Supination deformity and impaction of the cancellous bone at the dorsal fracture cortex.
Associated fracture of the ulnar styloid process is present in more than 50% of clinical cases.

blocks.title: Mechanism of injury and deformity
bullets: Caused by a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the wrist in dorsiflexion and forearm in pronation.
Produces the classic clinical dinner fork (bayonet) deformity described by Abraham Colles in 1814.
Distinguish from Smith fracture (reverse Colles): fall on flexed wrist causing palmar (volar) displacement and garden spade deformity.
Distinguish from Barton fracture: intra-articular fracture-subluxation of the radiocarpal joint with volar or dorsal displacement.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Closed reduction under haematoma block or Bier block followed by immobilization in a below-elbow Colles cast.
Cast position: slight flexion and ulnar deviation with neutral pronation; avoid extreme flexion to prevent median nerve compression.
Complications: malunion with dinner-fork deformity, carpal tunnel syndrome, Sudeck osteodystrophy (CRPS), and extensor pollicis longus tendon rupture.

viva.q: What are the six classic components of displacement in a Colles fracture?
viva.a: Dorsal displacement, dorsal tilt, radial displacement, radial tilt, supination, and proximal impaction of the distal cancellous radial fragment.

viva.q: How does a Smith fracture differ from a Colles fracture?
viva.a: Smith fracture (reverse Colles) results from a fall on the dorsum of a flexed wrist, producing volar (anterior) displacement and tilt (garden spade deformity).

viva.q: What late tendon complication can occur after a minimally displaced Colles fracture?
viva.a: Delayed rupture of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon, caused by avascular necrosis or friction over the irregular dorsal Lister tubercle.

image.brief: Anteroposterior and lateral wrist radiographs showing an extra-articular transverse fracture of the distal radius 2 cm proximal to the joint with dorsal tilt, radial shortening, and ulnar styloid fracture.

credit.author: Ashish j29

items.summary: Plain radiograph of pelvis with both hips showing discontinuity of femoral neck cortex, disruption of Shenton line, and external rotation deformity.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Discontinuity, step-off, or overlap of the bony cortices across the subcapital, transcervical, or basicervical region of femoral neck.
Disruption of Shenton line: the smooth continuous parabolic arc between lower margin of superior pubic ramus and medial femoral neck is broken.
Disruption of Ward triangle and trabecular arches crossing the femoral neck and head.
External rotation deformity: lesser trochanter appears unusually prominent on the injured side due to external rotation of femoral shaft.
Proximal migration of the greater trochanter above Nelaton line with limb shortening.

blocks.title: Classification and vascular supply
bullets: Garden classification: Stage I (incomplete/impacted), Stage II (complete non-displaced), Stage III (complete partially displaced), Stage IV (fully displaced).
Pauwels classification based on fracture line angle with horizontal: Type I (<30 deg), Type II (30-50 deg), Type III (>50 deg, high vertical shear).
Femoral head blood supply is retrograde via retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery in the joint capsule.
Intracapsular displacement tears retinacular vessels, leading to a high incidence of avascular necrosis (AVN) and non-union.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Distinguish from extracapsular trochanteric fracture: trochanteric fractures lie outside capsule, have rich blood supply, and rarely develop AVN.
Management in elderly patients with displaced fracture (Garden III/IV): hemiarthroplasty (bipolar) or total hip replacement (THA).
Management in young patients: urgent anatomic closed/open reduction and internal fixation with multiple cannulated cancellous screws.

viva.q: What is Shenton line and how is it interpreted on a pelvic radiograph?
viva.a: A smooth continuous curved line drawn along the inferior border of superior pubic ramus and continuous with the medial margin of femoral neck; disruption indicates fracture or dislocation.

viva.q: Why is avascular necrosis (AVN) a major risk in intracapsular neck of femur fractures?
viva.a: Because the primary blood supply to the femoral head arises from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery which are torn by displaced intracapsular fractures.

viva.q: What is the Garden classification for femoral neck fractures?
viva.a: Stage I is incomplete or impacted; Stage II is complete non-displaced; Stage III is complete with partial displacement; Stage IV is completely displaced with lost trabecular alignment.

image.brief: Anteroposterior pelvis and hip radiograph demonstrating a displaced transcervical fracture of the right femoral neck with broken Shenton line, prominent lesser trochanter, and varus angulation.

credit.author: Booyabazooka

aka: Giant cell tumour of bone on radiograph
items.summary: Plain radiograph demonstrating an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion in the epiphyseo-metaphyseal region of a long bone with classic soap-bubble trabeculations.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Eccentrically located, purely osteolytic radiolucent lesion situated in the epiphyseo-metaphyseal region of a skeletally mature long bone.
Expansile remodeling with thinning of the overlying cortical bone ('egg-shell crackling' thinning) extending right up to subchondral bone.
Internal pseudotrabeculation creating the classic 'soap-bubble' or honeycomb radiological appearance.
Conspicuous absence of osteosclerotic reactive rim, bone matrix calcification, or periosteal new bone reaction (no Codman triangle).

blocks.title: Demographics, anatomical sites, and behavior
bullets: Most common in young adults aged 20 to 40 years with fused growth plates (skeletal maturity), with slight female preponderance.
Most frequent anatomical sites: lower end of femur, upper end of tibia (around the knee in 50% to 60%), and lower end of radius.
Typically benign but locally aggressive with a high rate of local recurrence (approximately 20% to 30% after simple curettage).
Can metastasize to the lungs in 2% of histologically benign cases ('benign pulmonary metastases').

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Campanacci grading: Grade 1 (quiescent, intra-osseous), Grade 2 (active, thinned expanded cortex), Grade 3 (aggressive, cortical breach).
Standard surgical treatment is extended curettage using high-speed burr and chemical adjuvant (phenol or liquid nitrogen) with bone grafting or cement.
Campanacci Grade 3 lesions or expendable bones (proximal fibula, distal ulna) are managed by wide en bloc resection.

viva.q: What are the cardinal radiological features of a giant cell tumour of bone (osteoclastoma)?
viva.a: An eccentric, expansile, purely lytic epiphyseo-metaphyseal lesion in a skeletally mature bone, extending to subchondral bone with soap-bubble trabeculations and no sclerosis.

viva.q: What are the commonest anatomical locations for giant cell tumours?
viva.a: The lower end of the femur and upper end of the tibia (around the knee joint), followed by the lower end of the radius and sacrum.

viva.q: What is meant by 'extended curettage' in the surgical treatment of osteoclastoma?
viva.a: Mechanical curettage followed by high-speed burring of the cavity wall and application of local adjuvants like phenol, liquid nitrogen, or bone cement to eliminate microscopic disease.

image.brief: Plain anteroposterior and lateral knee radiograph showing an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion in the medial condyle of the distal femur extending to the subchondral plate with soap-bubble pattern.

items.summary: Plain radiograph demonstrating a mixed osteolytic and sclerotic lesion in the metaphysis of a long bone with sunray spiculation and Codman triangle.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Centrally located, poorly defined destructive lesion in the metaphysis of a long bone with mixed lytic and dense blastic areas.
Cortical destruction with breakthrough of the bony cortex and extension into the surrounding soft tissues forming a soft tissue mass.
Codman triangle: reactive triangular periosteal elevation at the periphery where the tumour elevates periosteum away from cortex.
Sunray (sunburst) spiculation: delicate radial radiating spicules of reactive and neoplastic bone oriented perpendicularly to shaft.
Wide zone of transition with permeative or moth-eaten bone destruction merging imperceptibly into normal marrow.

blocks.title: Demographics, anatomical distribution, and spread
bullets: Primary peak incidence occurs in the second decade of life (10 to 20 years) during the adolescent growth spurt.
Secondary peak occurs in elderly patients, associated with Paget disease of bone or prior radiation therapy.
Most frequent sites are the rapidly growing metaphyseal regions: lower end of femur, upper end of tibia, and upper end of humerus.
Spreads haematogenously early, with a strong predilection for the lungs ('cannonball metastases') and bones (skip lesions).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Staging requires contrast-enhanced MRI of the entire involved bone (to detect skip lesions) and high-resolution chest CT for lung deposits.
Biopsy technique: longitudinal incision centered directly over the planned future surgical resection tract to avoid contamination.
Modern management: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, followed by limb-salvage surgery (wide local excision with modular endoprosthesis), and adjuvant chemotherapy.

viva.q: What causes the sunray (sunburst) spiculation in osteosarcoma?
viva.a: Rapid tumor growth elevates the periosteum, stimulating osteoblasts to lay down new bone along the vertically oriented Sharpey fibers and periosteal blood vessels.

viva.q: What is Codman triangle and is it pathognomonic for osteosarcoma?
viva.a: A triangular wedge of reactive periosteal new bone formed where periosteum is stripped by advancing tumour; it is a sign of aggressive periosteal elevation, not exclusively specific to osteosarcoma.

viva.q: What is the standard protocol for limb-salvage surgery in osteosarcoma today?
viva.a: Three cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, restaging, wide en bloc resection of tumour with negative margins, reconstruction with modular mega-prosthesis, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy.

image.brief: Plain radiograph of the distal femur showing a mixed lytic and sclerotic metaphyseal lesion with cortical breach, delicate radiating sunburst spicules, and a peripheral Codman triangle.

credit.author: Joel Mills
